questions.question: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding and a pelvic mass. An ultrasound reveals a solid ovarian mass. The mass is surgically removed, and the HPE shows small, follicle-like structures filled with eosinophilic material. Which histological feature is most likely associated with this ovarian tumour?

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and histopathological findings are consistent with a Granulosa cell tumour, a sex cord-stromal tumour. Call-Exner bodies are small, follicle-like structures filled with eosinophilic material in the lumen of the follicles, characteristic of granulosa cell tumours.

Types of Sex cord - stromal tumors of Ovary: Feature Sertoli-Leydig tumour, Pure Leydig tumour (or Hilus cell tumour) Fibroma, Thecoma, Fibrothecoma Granulosa Cell Tumor Derived from Sertoli or Leydig cells Ovarian stroma Granulosa cells of ovarian follicle Age of Occurrence Second and third decades Any age Postmenopausal (adult type), any age (juvenile type) Associated symptoms Abnormal sexual development or Virilization Associated with Meigs syndrome ( triad of benign ovarian fibroma + ascites+ pleural effusion) and basal nevus syndrome Precocious sexual development in juveniles or abnormal uterine bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia (carcinoma) in adults Histological features Reinke crystalloids (in pure Leydig cell tumours) Well-differentiated fibroblasts (fibroma), plump spindle cells with lipid droplets (thecomas) Call-Exner bodies, Coffee bean nuclei Mutations & Markers Mutations in DICER1 (which encodes endonuclease) Vimentin +, Thecoma: Oil Red O +ve Fibroma: Oil Red O -ve Elevated inhibin levels, CD99+, and FOXL2 mutations (in adult cases) Prognosis Low recurrence or metastasis rate (<5%) Benign; Rarely malignant (fibrosarcomas) Potentially malignant with unpredictable behaviour; 10-year survival rate 85%

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal pain and a rapidly enlarging pelvic mass. Imaging reveals a solid and cystic ovarian tumour. A biopsy of the mass shows immature neural elements and other embryonic-like tissues, indicating a high risk of malignancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Types of Teratoma Mature Teratoma (aka Dermoid cyst): Benign ovarian tumour comprising tissues from all three germ layers. Immature Teratoma: Ovarian tumour with immature or embryonic-like tissues associated with an increased risk of malignancy. Monodermal Teratoma: Tumor primarily consists of a single tissue type, like thyroid tissue in struma ovarii or neuroendocrine cells in carcinoid tumours.

questions.question: A 16-year-old female presents with abdominal pain, distension, and a large pelvic mass accompanied by ascites. Elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein levels are detected. Surgical resection of the mass reveals histopathological findings depicted in the image. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanation.text: Given clinical presentation of 16 year old female with abdominal pain and ascites along with elevated serum AFP and HPE showing shiller duval bodies points towards Endodermal sinus tumor. Most common age group affected in germ cell tumours of ovary is 10-30 years of age Classification of Germ cell tumours: Tumour type Histological feature Endodermal Sinus Tumour Presence of Schiller-Duval bodies.

Dysgerminoma ‘Fried egg appearance’ (large cells with clear cytoplasm and central nuclei). Lymphocytic infiltration in the fibrous septa. Choriocarcinoma Consists of cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts. It may show haemorrhage and necrosis. Teratoma They comprise tissues from all three germ cell layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm), such as skin, hair,teeth, and neural tissue.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with irregular menstrual cycles and difficulty conceiving undergoes an endometrial biopsy. HPE reveals glands with tall columnar epithelial cells with subnuclear vacuoles. Which phase of the endometrial cycle is most likely being discussed here?

explanation.text: **Phase Day Morphological changes Proliferative phase (Option A):** Day 5-14 The rapid growth of glands and stroma from the basalis layer and tall columnar cells with numerous mitotic figures are seen. Absence of mucus secretion or vacuolation. Stroma is composed of spindle cells with minimal cytoplasm. Ovulatory phase Day 14 Mature follicle rupture and releases oocyte. Watery mucus is produced in the cervix, which facilitates sperm passage Secretory phase Day 14-28 Early secretory phase: Presence of subnuclear vacuolation in the glandular epithelium. ( Option B) Late secretory phase: Basal vacuoles gradually move to the apical surface. Glands become tortuous. (Serrated or Sawtooth appearance) Stromal changes include stromal cell hypertrophy infiltration of neutrophils and lymphocytes. (Option C) Menstrual phase Day 1-5 Breakdown of the corpus luteum and the subsequent drop in progesterone levels. The functional layer of the endometrium breaks down, leading to bleeding within the stroma and the start of the next menstrual cycle. (Option D)

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with persistent dull lower abdominal pain and increased urinary frequency. A uterine ultrasound reveals a heterogeneous vascular mass with areas of necrosis. Biopsy results show spindle cells with significant atypia, high mitotic activity, and necrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The patient most likely has uterine leiomyosarcoma, a malignant smooth muscle tumour of the myometrium.

**Characteristic Leiomyoma (Fibroid) (Option C):** Leiomyosarcoma (Option D) Type Benign smooth muscle tumour of the myometrium. Malignant smooth muscle tumour of the myometrium. Gene mutations MED12 gene Highly variable Cellular Atypia Minimal to absent Prominent Mitotic Activity Rare to absent Increased, >10/10 hpf Gross Pattern Well-defined, encapsulated, whorled, firm, grey-white tumours varying in size Bulky masses that invade the uterine wall OR Polypoid masses that project into the lumen Microscopic Features Uniform bundles of smooth muscle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei. Characterised by spindle shaped smooth muscle cells with nuclear atypia, high mitotic index and tumour necrosis. Necrosis Absent Often present Risk of Metastasis Virtually absent Can metastasise, particularly to the lungs Endometriosis (Option A) presents with heavy menstrual bleeding accompanied by severe menstrual pain due to ectopic endometrial tissue Endometrial cancer (Option B) presents with irregular uterine bleeding and hpe shows atypical tortuous uterine glands

questions.question: A 30-year-old pregnant woman at 20 weeks gestation presents with acute onset of severe abdominal pain. On examination, she has a tender, firm uterine mass. Ultrasound shows a fibroid with heterogeneous echotexture and increased vascularity. What type of degeneration is most likely occurring in the fibroid?

explanation.text: The patient most likely has red degeneration of fibroids, characterised by prominent blood vessels and haemorrhage due to inadequate blood supply to the fibroid due to its sudden rapid growth.

Fibroids can be classified based on their location: Intramural myomas Submucosal myomas Subserosal myomas Cervical myomas Types of Degeneration in Uterine Fibroids Fibroid degeneration can occur when the fibroid grows too quickly and outpaces its blood supply, or when the feeder arteries are mechanically compressed. Hyaline Degeneration: Most common (60% of cases). Fibroid tissue appears glassy.

Calcification Degeneration: Calcium deposits harden the fibroid. Common in older women; leads to non-functioning fibroids. Cystic Degeneration: Formation of cysts, typically after menopause. Myxoid Degeneration: Fibroid filled with jelly-like substance. Red Degeneration: Occurs during pregnancy. Symptoms: Severe nausea, vomiting, and vaginal bleeding.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic discomfort, and increased urinary frequency. Examination reveals an enlarged, irregular uterus, and imaging shows well-defined, solid myometrial masses.Which of the following genetic rearrangements is seen in leiomyomas?

explanation.text: The clinical scenario points towards Leiomyoma, (aka fibroid) a benign smooth muscle tumour of the myometrium causing symptoms like heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic discomfort, and increased urinary frequency, caused by rearrangements in the MED12 gene on chromosomes 12q and 6p. They are well-defined, whorled, firm, grey-white tumours varying in size.
Microscopically, there are uniform bundles of smooth muscle cells arranged in whorls with cigar-shaped nuclei.

questions.question: Which of the following genetic mutations is associated with Endometrial hyperplasia?

explanation.text: PTEN gene inactivation is seen in both endometrial hyperplasia and endometrioid endometrial carcinoma. PTEN produces a lipid phosphatase, which is a suppressor of the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT growth signalling pathway. Loss of PTEN function leads to excessive activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, contributing to endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Germline mutation of PTEN,present on chromosome 10 is known as Cowden syndrome.

Gene Mutations and Associated Cancers Endometrial Hyperplasia & Endometrioid (Type 1) Endometrial Carcinoma: PIK3CA, FGFR2, ARID1A, MYC, BRAF BRCA1/BRCA2 Cancers: Breast, Ovarian, Prostate, Pancreatic, Uterine Serous Adenocarcinoma (Type 2) TP53 Cancers: Breast, Colorectal, Ovarian, Uterine Serous Adenocarcinoma (Type 2)

questions.question: Which of the following statements is NOT true about Adenomyosis?

options.A: It presents with abnormal uterine bleeding.
options.B: Ectopic endometrial tissue is found at least 2.5 cm from the endometrial junction.
options.C: It is seen in pre-menopausal women.
options.D: Biopsy shows irregular nests of endometrial stroma arranged within the myometrium.

explanation.text: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial tissue within the myometrium at least 2.5 mm away from the endometrial / endomyometrial junction (not 2.5 cm).
**It is typically seen in pre-menopausal, multiparous women in their 30-40’s (Option C):** and is associated with a history of prior uterine surgery like C-section and increased exposure to estrogen.

**Clinical presentation includes Irregular and heavy menstrual bleeding (menometrorrhagia) (Option A):** Crampy menstrual pain (dysmenorrhea) Pain during intercourse (dyspareunia) Pelvic discomfort, particularly before menstruation.

**HPE shows irregular nests of endometrial stroma arranged within the myometrium (Option D):** On per abdominal examination, uterus is tender and enlarged uniformly upto size of 12 weeks pregnant uterus Initial investigation is USG MRI is IOC- The most established MRI finding for adenomyosis is a junctional zone that's thicker than 12 mm. TOC is hysterectomy Adenomyosis MRI: can show salt and pepper appearance.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with chronic pelvic pain worsened during menstrual periods and accompanied by heavy bleeding, was found to have a 'chocolate' brown cyst on her ovaries during a laparoscopy. What is the most commonly accepted theory for the pathogenesis of this condition?

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and presence of a chocolate brown cyst on the ovaries suggest Endometriosis. This condition often occurs due to retrograde menstruation through the fallopian tubes, which frequently occurs, leading to the implantation of endometrial tissue at ectopic sites due to the backward flow of menstrual endometrium.
The regurgitation theory (Sampson’s theory) explains the presence of ectopic endometrial tissue in the peritoneal cavity, which is present in most cases; thus, it is widely accepted.

**Benign metastasis theory (Halban’s theory) (Option A):** The benign metastasis theory suggests that endometrial tissue from the uterus can disseminate to distant locations, such as the bone, lungs, and brain, through blood vessels and lymphatic channels.

**Metaplastic theory (Meyer and Ivanoff’s theory) (Option B):** The metaplastic theory suggests that endometrial tissue can develop directly from the coelomic epithelium, which is the embryonic origin of the Mullerian ducts and the endometrium.
**Extrauterine stem/progenitor cell theory (Option C):** The Extrauterine stem/progenitor cell theory suggests that progenitor cells from the bone marrow differentiate into endometrial tissue.

questions.question: What is the role of inhibin?

explanation.text: Inhibin from the granulosa cells inhibits FSH secretion. It is a hormone primarily produced by the ovaries (in females) and testes (in males). It regulates the reproductive system by inhibiting the secretion of FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone) from the anterior pituitary gland.

Inhibin suppresses the FSH Inhibin B: Before ovulation Inhibin A: After ovulation Stimulates the secretion of FSH (Option A): Inhibin does not stimulate FSH release; instead, it inhibits it. FSH is involved in the growth and maturation of reproductive cells, but inhibin reduces its secretion once the follicle or sperm production reaches sufficient levels.

**Inhibition of PRL (Option C) and Stimulation of PRL (Option D):** Inhibin does not directly regulate prolactin (PRL), a hormone involved in milk production. PRL levels are primarily controlled by dopamine from the hypothalamus and other factors, not by inhibin. Therefore, inhibin neither inhibits nor stimulates PRL production.

questions.question: In the cervical smear below, which of the following stains are used

explanation.text: Papanicolaou stain is the standard stain used in cervical smears to detect cellular abnormalities.

The Pap stain results in: Well-stained nuclear chromatin Differential polychromatic counterstaining of the cytoplasm Cytoplasmic transparency H & E stain (Option B) ( hematoxylin and eosin) staining procedure uses two dyes to stain tissue samples, making it easier to see cell structure under a microscope; this is commonly used for histopathological tissue sections, not for cervical smears.
**Giemsa stain (Option C):** is used to stain blood and bone marrow smears, as well as some parasites, but it is not used in cervical cytology.

**Toluidine blue (Option D):** is a basic metachromatic dye primarily used to stain acidic components of tissues, such as nucleic acids and mast cell granules. It is not used for routine cervical cytology.

These serotypes are known to cause condyloma acuminatum and are commonly associated with laryngeal lesions, particularly in children and young adults Types of HPV Cutaneous involvement HPV 1, 2, 3 (low risk) Filiform wart Verruca Plantaris HPV 5, 8 (high risk) Epidermodysplasia Verruciformis Mucosal involvement HPV 6, 11 (low risk) Condyloma Acuminatum Recurrent laryngeal papillomas HPV 16, 18, 31, 33, 35 (high risk) Squamous cell carcinoma HPV 16 ( High risk) LSIL, HSIL, Carcinoma cervix Vulval carcinoma Oropharyngeal SCC HPV 18 ( High risk) LSIL, HSIL, Carcinoma cervix Anogenital carcinoma Cutaneous involvement Benign Warts Common Skin Warts (Verruca Vulgaris): Small, hard, rough growths on the skin; commonly seen in children (associated with serotypes 2, 4, 27, 57).

Associated with serotypes 5, 8, 9, 12, 17, 20, 36, and 47. Mucosal involvement Anogenital Warts It is also known as Condyloma Acuminatum.

A sexually transmitted infection in adults, associated with HPV serotypes 6 and 11. Head and Neck Lesions Benign: Recurrent laryngeal papillomas, especially in children (serotypes 6, 11 ). Serotype 16 alone accounts for ~50% of cases, while serotypes 16 & 18 together cause ~70% of cervical cancers.

questions.question: What is the most probable tumour that a 22-year-old woman with a sizable growth in her right ovary, which has been determined to originate from all three germ layers based on histopathology, is experiencing?

explanation.text: Teratomas are tumours that originate from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm) and are commonly found in the ovaries. They are often seen in young women and can contain a variety of tissue types, such as hair, teeth, and muscle, which reflects their origin from all three germ layers.

Immature teratoma: Bulky, solid ovarian tumours that contain immature neuroepithelium, cartilage, bone, and muscle, with areas of necrosis and haemorrhage. They grow rapidly, often spreading beyond the ovary. They are seen in young females and have a high risk of malignancy. They have small, round blue cells (Immature neural components). Mature teratoma Mature teratomas, or dermoid cysts, are common benign ovarian tumours found in young women.

They are bilateral in 10-15% of cases. They contain tissues from all three germ layers, including skin, hair, and teeth, and can rarely undergo malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Grossly, they are unilocular cysts with a thin wall and hair; microscopically, they have stratified squamous epithelium and sebaceous glands.

Monodermal teratoma: Monodermal teratomas consist predominantly of a single type of tissue, such as thyroid tissue in struma ovarii or neuroendocrine cells in carcinoid tumours. They lack immature or embryonic-like tissues and typically do not have a high risk of malignancy.

**Dysgerminoma (Option A):** is also a type of germ cell tumour (GCT) that typically secretes beta hCG. Thecoma (Option C) is a rare benign tumour originating from the ovarian stroma, accounting for less than 1% of all ovarian tumours. It is most commonly found in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women.
**Theca lutein cysts (Option D):** are rare benign cystic lesions caused by hypertrophy of the theca interna layer due to excessive stimulation by hCG.

questions.question: What is the most likely diagnosis for a 48-year-old patient who came with scrotal swelling, had elevated LDH levels but normal AFP levels on tests for testicular tumours, and exhibited a specific histological picture after orchidectomy?

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and histopathological findings suggest testicular seminoma. Seminomas elevate LDH levels, while AFP remains normal. Histology shows large, uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. Seminoma: It is the most common germ cell tumour of the testis. A similar presentation in the ovary is called dysgerminoma, and germinoma is present in the pineal gland. Incidence: Peak incidence in the fourth decade.

Genetics: Seminomas contain isochromosome 12p and express OCT3/4 & NANOG. Morphology: Seminoma has a homogeneous, grey-white, lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of haemorrhage or necrosis. Histology of seminoma: Sheets of monomorphic cells. The sheets are divided into poorly demarcated lobules by the septa of the fibrous tissue. The septa show lymphocytic infiltration (T lymphocytes).

The classic seminoma cell is large and round to polyhedral with a distinct cell membrane and a large, central nucleus with one or two prominent nucleoli. The cytoplasm is clear or watery appearing and contains glycogen. The arrows in the image below show seminomatous tumour cells.
